sections.title: Introduction
rules: Many machine learning problems process temporal sequences or spatial patterns.
Examples include speech recognition, natural language processing, and biological sequence analysis.
Successive observations in a sequence exhibit strong statistical dependencies.
We need models that capture dependencies across time.
Hidden Markov Models provide a probabilistic framework for sequence modeling.

sections.title: Discrete Markov Processes
rules: A system exists in one of N distinct states at each time step.
At discrete time intervals, the system changes state according to transition probabilities.
A first-order Markov process assumes the next state depends only on the current state.
Transition probability a_ij is the probability of moving from state i to state j.
State transition probabilities must be non-negative and sum to one for each state.
The initial state distribution defines the probability of starting in each state.
In an observable Markov model, the states are directly visible to the observer.

sections.title: Hidden Markov Models
rules: In a Hidden Markov Model, the actual states are not directly observable.
The underlying state sequence is a hidden stochastic process.
In each state, the system emits an observable symbol from a discrete alphabet.
The emission probability b_j(k) is the probability of observing symbol k in state j.
An HMM has two stochastic layers: hidden state transitions and visible symbol emissions.
A complete model contains the transition matrix, the emission matrix, and initial probabilities.

sections.title: Three Basic Problems of HMMs
rules: Problem 1 is evaluation: Calculate the probability that a model generated an observed sequence.
Problem 2 is decoding: Find the most likely hidden state sequence for an observed sequence.
Problem 3 is learning: Adjust model parameters to maximize the probability of observed training sequences.
We must solve these three problems to use HMMs in practical applications.

sections.title: Evaluation Problem
rules: Direct evaluation requires summing probabilities across all possible hidden state sequences.
Direct computation requires exponential time and is impractical for long sequences.
The forward algorithm uses dynamic programming to solve the evaluation problem efficiently.
The forward variable alpha_t(i) is the joint probability of past observations and current state i.
We calculate forward variables recursively from the first time step to the last.
The backward algorithm computes probabilities backwards from the final time step.
The backward variable beta_t(i) represents the probability of remaining observations given state i.
Both forward and backward algorithms run in polynomial time proportional to sequence length.

sections.title: Finding the State Sequence
rules: Decoding identifies the optimal sequence of hidden states that explains the observations.
Finding the best state at each time step independently can produce invalid transitions.
The Viterbi algorithm finds the single best global state path through dynamic programming.
The Viterbi variable delta_t(i) stores the maximum probability along a path ending in state i.
Backtracking pointers record the preceding state that maximized the transition probability.
After reaching the final time step, we trace pointers backward to retrieve the optimal path.
The Viterbi algorithm runs in quadratic time with respect to the number of states.

sections.title: Learning Model Parameters
rules: In the learning problem, we train model parameters from observed sequences without state labels.
The Baum-Welch algorithm is an Expectation-Maximization method for HMM parameter estimation.
In the E-step, we compute expected state visits and expected transitions using forward-backward variables.
In the M-step, we update transition probabilities, emission probabilities, and initial probabilities.
Each iteration of Baum-Welch guarantees non-decreasing likelihood of the observed data.
The algorithm stops when parameter changes fall below a small threshold.
We apply scaling factors to forward and backward variables to prevent numerical underflow.

sections.title: Continuous Observations
rules: In many tasks, observations are continuous feature vectors rather than discrete symbols.
We replace discrete emission probabilities with continuous probability density functions.
A Gaussian distribution models continuous observation vectors for each state.
When state emissions are complex, we use Gaussian Mixture Models.
The learning algorithm re-estimates mixture weights, mean vectors, and covariance matrices.

sections.title: The HMM with Input
rules: An input-output HMM conditions state transitions and emissions on external input sequences.
External inputs influence state dynamics at each time step.
This architecture models sequence transduction and conditioned temporal responses.
We can implement transition and emission mappings with generalized linear models or neural networks.

sections.title: Model Selection in HMM
rules: Model topology defines allowable transitions between hidden states.
An ergodic model permits transitions between all pairs of states.
A left-to-right model only allows transitions to current or subsequent states.
Left-to-right topologies model irreversible temporal processes such as spoken phonemes.
We select the number of hidden states using cross-validation or Bayesian information criteria.

sections.title: Notes
rules: Hidden Markov Models became the primary technology for automatic speech recognition systems.
Molecular biologists use HMMs for sequence alignment and gene finding in DNA.
Extensions include factorial HMMs and hidden semi-Markov models for variable state durations.
